name: NPL caesium atomic clock
description: Louis Essen and J. V. L. Parry built a caesium atomic clock at the National Physical Laboratory in Teddington, using an atomic transition as a timekeeping reference.

impact.note: First working clock of its kind, keeping time by an atomic transition better than astronomy could; used by metrologists, it led to atomic time scales and the redefined second.

date.label: January 1953
date.basis: Whibberley dates Essen’s receipt of travel funding to January 1953; this is not a date of a working NPL clock.

events.statement: Essen received funding from a US State Department-administered aid programme to visit US atomic-clock laboratories. After returning he was authorized to begin the NPL clock project.

evidence.locator: p. 34, origins of the NPL project
evidence.supports: Dates the travel funding and distinguishes subsequent approval from the earlier shortage of skilled staff.

contributions.resource: Administration of the aid programme funding Essen’s research visits; not an assertion that the department financed the complete clock.

evidence.supports: Identifies the State Department as administrator of the aid programme.

date.label: May 1955
date.basis: NIST dates the unveiling to May 1955; the museum attributes the 1955 clock to Essen and Parry.

events.statement: The NPL caesium clock built by Essen and Parry was unveiled in May 1955.

evidence.supports: Identifies Essen, Parry, NPL, Teddington and 1955.
Dates the unveiling to May 1955 and describes earlier research and the Ramsey design.
Attributes the device to J. V. L. Parry.

contributions.resource: 5 MHz quartz oscillator used in the microwave synthesis chain of the completed 1955 apparatus; delivery date and terms not stated.

evidence.supports: Identifies a low-phase-noise 5 MHz oscillator obtained from the Marconi company.

earliest_record.rationale: The inspected evidence establishes the May 1955 unveiling, not the first conception or universal first atomic clock. The earlier travel-support event concerns enabling research, not an extant clock.

measures.subject: The 1955 NPL caesium clock
measures.conditions: Museum retrospective gives an equivalent rate; it does not report a 300-year observation or specify the measurement interval.

evidence.supports: Reports accuracy equivalent to one second in 300 years.

caveats: NIST describes an earlier ammonia-based atomic clock; the present record is the specific NPL caesium apparatus, not a global first claim. Later SI definition did not require adoption of this one device. The 1953 aid programme funded research travel; no total project budget or supplier payment terms are inferred.

research.note: Independent parent checked SMG object1962-59 and NIST historical sections. Performance remains a catalogue claim; NPL is host rather than an inferred separate developer or funder. Parent also checked Whibberley 2017 pp. 34–35 for the Ramsey-method link; added travel support and oscillator supply as separately scoped sourced contributions. Independent review reopened Whibberley pp. 34–35 and the SMG and NIST descriptions; January 1953 is the travel-funding receipt, while NIST dates the unveiling to May 1955. Marconi supplied the quartz oscillator; payment terms remain unknown.

organizations.note: Laboratory where the instrument was built; funding not inferred.

links.statement: The 1955 NPL apparatus used the separated-oscillatory-field method developed by Ramsey.
links.scope: The caesium-beam apparatus unveiled in 1955; link is to the method, not proof that a particular publication was consulted.

evidence.supports: Identifies the separated interactions in this apparatus with Ramsey’s 1949 method.
